title: Ribollita
subtitle: Tuscan bread and vegetable soup
excerpt: The great Tuscan peasant soup: cannellini beans, cavolo nero, and vegetables thickened with day-old bread until it is more stew than soup. Ribollita means reboiled: it improves on the second day.

recipe.sourceNotes: Ribollita is one of the defining dishes of Tuscan cucina povera, the tradition of simple, cheap, filling cooking developed by the poor of central Italy over centuries. The name means reboiled: traditionally it was made from leftover minestrone or bean soup, to which stale bread was added and the whole thing was reboiled the next day. The bread thickens and dissolves into the soup, creating a dense, porridge-like texture that is unique to this dish. Cavolo nero, the dark Tuscan kale, is the characteristic vegetable.

recipeTools.notes: Wide, heavy pot for the soup.

content.text: The bread is not a garnish added at the end: it goes into the soup with 20 minutes left and breaks down as it cooks, thickening the whole pot into a dense, spoonable stew. Use stale sourdough or white country bread with the crusts on. Do not skimp on the olive oil: ribollita should have a good drizzle of high-quality extra virgin oil poured over each bowl before serving.

Heat 60 ml of the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion, carrot, and celery with a pinch of salt. Cook for 12 minutes until soft. Add the garlic, rosemary, and thyme and cook for 2 minutes.

Add the tinned tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes. Add three-quarters of the beans. Mash the remaining beans roughly with a fork and add them too (they help thicken the soup). Add the stock. Simmer for 20 minutes.
Add the cavolo nero and torn bread. Stir well. Simmer for 20 more minutes, stirring occasionally, until the bread has broken down and the soup is very thick. Season generously.
Remove the herb sprigs. Serve in deep bowls with a generous drizzle of your best extra virgin olive oil and plenty of black pepper. The soup improves on reheating the next day.
